newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan's popularity at risk if Fed hikes in May.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan's popularity at risk if Fed hikes in May.

text.p: If Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan does hike interest rates at next week's meeting, he could be putting more at risk than just the nation's economic health -- his own popularity may be at stake.

"The biggest factor (arguing against a rate hike) is that Greenspan wants to be able to live comfortably in Washington and not have Congress beating down his door," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"It would really unleash the wrath of Congress if he moved again," he added.
Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, agreed and questioned why Greenspan would "unnecessarily stick his hand in a bear cage."

Senator Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, summed up the stance of Capitol Hill opponents who say higher rates will hamper the budget process when he reportedly quipped that there have been more sightings of Elvis than of rising inflation.
And Greenspan won't be able to turn to Wall Street for overwhelming support.

Economists here, who often spend more time trying to figure out what the Fed will do than why, have almost given up trying to read poker-faced Greenspan and can't seem to find any clear-cut answers in the numbers.

"In the last year, more than any other time in history, analysts have just said, 'I don't know'," said Christopher Rupkey, financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, recalling the September 1996 Federal Open Market Committee meeting where sentiment in financial circles was almost evenly divided.
"The problem that analysts are having is that they don't necessarily share the Fed's fear of future inflation," he added.

But the harshest critics this time around most likely would be the general public who is thriving from tight labor markets and roaring economic growth, but not smelling even a whiff of inflation, analysts said.

Greenspan himself exaccerbated the public-perception problem by saying in a high-profile speech last week that economic growth will taper off in the latter part of this year from the first-quarter's brisk 5.6 percent clip.
"The public wouldn't quite get it if the Fed tightens again after he told you he expects things to slow down," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Greenspan said the most "probable forecast" was for "moderate growth and low inflation for later this year and next."

"That's what I don't get. All these (Wall Street) experts are forecasting 2.0-percent growth this quarter and retail sales going down, so what is Greenspan thinking? That he better raise rates before the rationale disappears?," said a foreign exchange trader at a European bank in New York.

However, Greenspan proved he's not easily swayed by public opinion when he raised the federal funds rate on March 25 for the first time in more than two years and subsequently weathered a storm of criticism from naysayers both on Capitol Hill and Wall Street.
Greenspan was moved to take an atypical step and publicly defend his actions in his last speech.

Greenspan said he "raised rates as a form of insurance" and that it was "a small, prudent step in the face of the increasing possibility that excessive credit creation, spurred by an overly accommodative monetary policy, might undermine the sustained economic expansion."
"He certainly spent an awful lot of time trying to explain his way through the March 25 hike," Gilmore said.

But his rebuttal divided economists even further as one camp interpreted his defense as a sign he would not raise rates soon, while another thought it was an attempt to prep the markets for a second rate rise.

Former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker, who withstood his own share of criticism while at the helm of the central bank, said on Wednesday he was discouraged by the amount of criticism the Fed had endured for its March hike.
"We want to keep this process going in a very favorable way," Volcker said. "And that means taking precautionary ... moves so that inflation doesn't get out of hand."
